kinetic-energy-s1.title: One car at two speeds
kinetic-energy-s1.html: The car has a mass of 1200 kg. In both rows the driver brakes with the same braking force.

kinetic-energy-s2.title: Moving objects in a sports lab
kinetic-energy-s2.text: A class measures the mass and the speed of four moving objects.

table.caption: Mass and speed of four objects

items.q: What is the car's kinetic energy at 10 m/s? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the mass times the speed. Kinetic energy squares the speed and takes half: ½(1200 kg)(10 m/s)².

why.correct: K = ½mv² = ½(1200 kg)(10 m/s)² = 60,000 J = 6.0 × 10⁴ J. A joule is a kg·m²/s².

items.q: How does the car's kinetic energy at 20 m/s compare with its kinetic energy at 10 m/s?
options: 4 times as large
2 times as large
8 times as large
The same, since the mass is the same

why.correct: K = ½mv². The mass is fixed, so K ∝ v². Doubling v multiplies K by 2² = 4.
options: Right: K depends on v², and (20/10)² = 4.
This treats K as proportional to v. The speed is squared, so doubling it multiplies K by 4.
This cubes the speed ratio. K = ½mv² has v squared, not cubed.
The mass is the same, but K also depends on the speed, and the speed doubled.

items.q: By how much does the car's kinetic energy increase when it speeds up from 10 m/s to 20 m/s? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is ½m(Δv)². The change in K is ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²: square each speed first, then subtract.
Value: that is the kinetic energy at 20 m/s. Subtract the kinetic energy at 10 m/s to get the change.

why.correct: ΔK = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i² = ½(1200 kg)[(20 m/s)² − (10 m/s)²] = ½(1200)(300) J = 1.8 × 10⁵ J. Note this is three times ½m(Δv)².

items.q: With the same braking force, the car at 10 m/s stops in a distance d. In what distance does it stop from 20 m/s?
options: 2d
4d
d

why.correct: The same braking force gives the same deceleration a (Newton's second law). From v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0, Δx = v₀²/(2a), so doubling v₀ makes the distance 4 times as long, matching the four times larger kinetic energy.
options: This assumes the stopping distance grows in step with the speed. With constant deceleration it grows with v².
Right: the same force gives the same deceleration, and v² = 2aΔx makes the distance grow as v².
The deceleration is the same, but a faster car needs more distance to lose its speed.
This takes a square root of the speed ratio. The distance depends on v², so the factor is 2² = 4.

items.q: The car turns around and drives west at 20 m/s instead of east. Taking east as positive, what is its kinetic energy?
options: −2.4 × 10⁵ J, because the velocity is negative
Zero, because west cancels east
2.4 × 10⁵ J, the same as driving east
1.2 × 10⁵ J, half the eastward value

why.correct: K = ½(1200 kg)(−20 m/s)² = ½(1200)(400) J = 2.4 × 10⁵ J. Squaring removes the sign, so kinetic energy is a scalar with no direction.
options: The velocity is squared, so its sign drops out. Kinetic energy is a scalar that is never negative.
Directions do not cancel for one object's kinetic energy; it depends on the size of the velocity.
Right: kinetic energy depends on speed only, and the speed is still 20 m/s.
Changing direction does not change the speed, so nothing halves.

items.q: What is the tennis ball's kinetic energy, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies the mass by the speed. Kinetic energy is ½mv², with the speed squared.

items.q: How does the bowling ball's kinetic energy compare with the tennis ball's?
options: The bowling ball's is 100 times larger
The tennis ball's is 10 times larger
The bowling ball's is 10 times larger
They are equal

why.correct: Bowling ball: ½(6.0 kg)(5.0 m/s)² = 75 J. Tennis ball: 75 J. A small, fast object can carry as much kinetic energy as a big, slow one.
options: This compares masses alone. The tennis ball is 10 times faster, and the speed counts squared.
This treats K as proportional to speed. The speed ratio is squared: 10² = 100, which cancels the mass ratio.
This takes the mass ratio and divides by the speed ratio once. The speed ratio should be squared.
Right: both are 75 J. The bowling ball's 100 times larger mass is offset by a speed 10 times smaller, and 10² = 100.

items.q: Which comparison of the sprinter and the cyclist is correct?
options: The sprinter has about twice as much
The cyclist has more, because the cyclist has more mass
They have about the same kinetic energy
The sprinter has about 1.5 times as much

why.correct: Sprinter: ½(70. kg)(9.0 m/s)² ≈ 2.8 × 10³ J. Cyclist: ½(80. kg)(6.0 m/s)² ≈ 1.4 × 10³ J. The sprinter has about twice as much.
options: Right: 2.8 × 10³ J against 1.4 × 10³ J.
The cyclist is heavier, but the sprinter's speed is 1.5 times larger, and that counts squared: 1.5² = 2.25.
Work out both: ½(70)(81) ≈ 2.8 × 10³ J and ½(80)(36) ≈ 1.4 × 10³ J. They differ by a factor of about 2.
That is the speed ratio. Kinetic energy depends on the speed squared and on the mass.

items.q: How fast would the cyclist and bike (80. kg) have to move to have the same kinetic energy as the sprinter? Answer in m/s.

mistakes.why: Value: that divides K by m. Solve K = ½mv² for v: v = √(2K/m).
Value: you left out the 2. Solving K = ½mv² gives v = √(2K/m).

items.q: Which combination of SI base units is the same as a joule?
options: kg·m/s
kg·m²/s²
kg·m/s²
kg·m²/s

why.correct: A joule is kg·m²/s². Writing the units of ½mv² gives kg × m²/s².
options: That is the unit of mass times velocity, with the speed not squared.
Right: from K = ½mv², kg × (m/s)² = kg·m²/s².
That is a newton, the unit of force.
The time unit must be squared too, because the speed is squared.

items.q: A student finds that a 2.0 kg cart moving left at 3.0 m/s has a kinetic energy of −9.0 J. What went wrong?
options: Nothing: leftward motion has negative kinetic energy
The ½ was left out; it should be −4.5 J
K cannot be negative; it is +9.0 J
The speed should not be squared; it is −3.0 J

why.correct: K = ½mv² = ½(2.0 kg)(−3.0 m/s)² = +9.0 J. Kinetic energy is a scalar and is never negative.
options: Kinetic energy has no direction. Squaring the velocity removes its sign.
The ½ was used: ½(2.0)(9.0) = 9.0. The real slip is the sign.
Right: (−3.0 m/s)² is positive, so K = +9.0 J.
K = ½mv² does square the speed. The answer is positive.

items.q: A passenger sits still in a train that moves at 25 m/s along a straight track. Which statement about the passenger's kinetic energy is correct?
options: It is the same measured from the train and from the ground
It is zero in both frames because the passenger is sitting still
It is large in both frames because the train is moving
Zero in the train's frame, large in the ground's

why.correct: Relative to the train, v = 0 and K = 0. Relative to the ground, v = 25 m/s and K = ½m(25 m/s)². Always say which frame a kinetic energy is measured in.
options: Speed is different in different frames, and K depends on speed.
The passenger is still in the train's frame, but moves at 25 m/s in the ground's frame.
In the train's frame the passenger has zero speed, so K = 0 there.
Right: speed depends on the reference frame, so kinetic energy does too.

items.q: A 0.40 kg cart speeds up from 1.5 m/s to 2.5 m/s. By how much does its kinetic energy change, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: that is ½m(Δv)². Compute ½mv² at each speed, then subtract.
Value: that is the final kinetic energy. Subtract the starting kinetic energy.

items.q: A crate moving at 3.0 m/s has 54 J of kinetic energy. What is its mass, in kg?

mistakes.why: Value: the speed must be squared. m = 2K/v² = 2(54 J)/(3.0 m/s)².

items.q: A cart moving east at 3.0 m/s is stopped, then pushed west until it moves west at 3.0 m/s. Take east as positive. Compare the end with the start.

variables.name: The cart's kinetic energy
variables.why: The speed is 3.0 m/s at both moments and the mass is the same, so ½mv² is the same.

variables.name: The cart's speed
variables.why: Speed is the size of the velocity: 3.0 m/s at the start and at the end.

variables.name: The x-component of the cart's velocity
variables.why: It goes from +3.0 m/s to −3.0 m/s, a decrease of 6.0 m/s.

why.correct: Kinetic energy depends on speed, not direction. The velocity changed sign; the speed and K did not.

items.q: A truck has 3 times the mass of a car and moves at half the car's speed. What is the ratio of the truck's kinetic energy to the car's?

why.correct: K ∝ mv². The ratio is (3)(1/2)² = 3/4. The truck has less kinetic energy than the car.
options: This uses the speed ratio without squaring it.
This multiplies by the speed ratio's inverse. Half the speed reduces K, by a factor of 4.
The factor of 4 from the speed belongs in the denominator: the truck is slower.

items.q: Two 1.0 kg carts move toward each other, one east at 2.0 m/s and one west at 2.0 m/s. What is the kinetic energy of the two-cart system?
options: Zero, because the motions are opposite

why.correct: The kinetic energy of a system is the sum of its parts' kinetic energies: 2.0 J + 2.0 J = 4.0 J. Unlike velocities, they never cancel.
options: Velocities in opposite directions cancel as vectors, but kinetic energies are scalars and add.
Right: each cart has ½(1.0)(2.0)² = 2.0 J, and the scalars add.
That is one cart's kinetic energy. The system has both carts.
This treats one cart as moving at the carts' relative speed, 4.0 m/s: ½(1.0)(4.0)² = 8.0 J. Each cart's K comes from its own speed relative to the ground.
